disease_info: Specific Phobia is characterized by a marked, persistent fear of a clearly identifiable object or situation that is excessive or out of proportion to the actual risk, and that consistently provokes intense anxiety and avoidance. The feared stimulus is either actively avoided or endured with significant distress, and this pattern must last at least six months and cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Onset often follows a discrete frightening or painful event involving the stimulus, vicarious learning (e.g., witnessing others’ fear), or informational transmission, and the course tends to be chronic if untreated, with individuals often organizing their lives to minimize contact with the phobic trigger. It is distinguished from other anxiety disorders by the narrow, circumscribed nature of the fear and the absence of broader, unexpected panic attacks or pervasive worry about multiple domains.

narrative.personality: Justin is a pragmatic, hands-on problem solver who mixes disciplined planning with curiosity-driven tinkering and generally prefers structured independence in both work and hobbies.
narrative.stressor: About two and a half years ago, Justin was overseeing the installation of a new automated assembly line when a hydraulic lift unexpectedly failed, dropping a heavy component just a few feet from where he was standing and narrowly missing a junior technician he had been mentoring. Though no one was seriously injured, the incident shook his sense of control around large industrial machinery, something he had always prided himself on understanding and managing safely. In the months that followed, he increasingly arranged his project work so that others handled on-site commissioning and start-up while he confined himself to design, simulations, and meetings, gradually restructuring his job and even his DIY projects at home to avoid being near similar equipment. As it became harder to justify skipping key plant visits and his avoidance began to strain relationships with colleagues and limit his advancement to more hands-on leadership roles, his wife and a close coworker urged him to seek psychiatric help.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I know it doesn’t make sense, but I get an overwhelming fear whenever I have to be around certain industrial machines at the plant.”

narrative.personality: Jeffery is a hyper-organized, competitive young auditor who channels his restless energy into precision, efficiency, and constant self-optimization in both work and leisure.
narrative.stressor: Just over two years ago, during a weekend hike in the Texas Hill Country with coworkers, Jeffery was bitten by a large dog that broke free from its owner on a narrow trail, knocking him down and leaving him briefly pinned and convinced he would lose control of the situation. Although the physical wounds healed quickly and the dog’s vaccinations were up to date, the event clashed sharply with his usual sense of control and meticulous planning, leaving a strong emotional imprint. Over time he began subtly reorganizing his routines—changing running routes, declining friends’ invitations to outdoor events, and even avoiding clients’ offices where he knew dogs were present—until these workarounds grew so extensive that he was turning down engagements and skipping runs he once treated as non-negotiable. When he realized he was spending significant time and mental energy plotting how to avoid any chance encounters with dogs, and it started to interfere with both his job opportunities and his main coping outlet of distance running, he decided to seek psychiatric evaluation at the urging of a mentor who noticed his growing rigidity.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I have this intense, irrational fear whenever I might run into a dog, and it’s starting to control where I go and what I do.”

narrative.personality: Danny is an easygoing yet competitive, road-seasoned mentor who enjoys improvisation, creative hobbies, and sharing stories from decades of travel.
narrative.stressor: Around two and a half years ago, Danny experienced a sudden dizzy spell and brief loss of balance while climbing down from his truck’s cab at a remote rest stop, causing him to slip and bang his head on the step; the ER evaluation later suggested a mild vestibular issue, but no serious injury. The unexpected sensation of the ground “tilting” under him, combined with his age and years spent on the road, left him preoccupied with the idea that heights or elevated positions might trigger another incident where he could be seriously hurt or stranded. Gradually he began avoiding tasks that required climbing—like accessing high loading docks, overpasses with open catwalks, or even ladders for home projects—and he steered his new freight brokerage work away from jobs that might involve such environments, despite previously taking pride in going anywhere a load needed to go. When his avoidance started limiting the routes he could comfortably mentor new drivers on, and he found himself turning down family outings that involved observation decks or stadium seating, his wife and an old driving buddy convinced him that his world had shrunk enough that it was time to talk to a mental health professional.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I go out of my way to avoid any kind of height now, and it’s starting to get in the way of both work and normal life.”
